latin.125: Superest ultima eius ratio ducta ab imputatione Iustitiae Christi. Eam sic concipit. Quod doctrinam de imputata Christi justitia vel convellit, vel labefactat, neque admittendum, neque tolerandum est, sed amolendum omnino ac rejiciendum. Atqui dogmate de Non-imputatione peccati Adae, doctrinam de imputatione justitiae Christi, non parum labefactari certum est, cum ex negatione prioris facillimus sit lapsus ad posterioris negationem. Nam cum in Christo tanquam secundo Adamo, remedium habeamus certissimum adversus ea mala & damna, quae sunt in genus humanum a primo Adamo invecta; Remedium autem morbis, quibus sanandis paratum est, justa proportione respondere debeat; qui praeter nativam corruptionem, nihil nos damni ex Adamo trahere existimabit, & huic corruptioni considerabit ex adverso respondere donum sanctificationis, facile in eam sententiam deveniet, cum nullus sit in nobis propter Adae inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, neque opus esse ulla justitia Christi imputatione, quae sanctificationem ordine naturae praecedat: quia ubi nullum est malum, nullo etiam opus est remedio.
latin.126: Nego dogma de Non-imputatione peccati Adae antecedente seu immediata ullo modo doctrinam de imputatione justitiae Christi labefactare; mihique valde dolet, quod videam virum doctum, ut id probet, deserere doctrinam de corruptionis nativae reatu, publicis fidei confessionibus Ecclesiarum protestantium declaratam, & confirmatam. Corruptio nativa duobus modis spectari potest: uno forensi, altero morali. Priori modo consideratur ut peccatum nobis damnandis sufficiens: Posteriori vero ut qualitas nos sua inhaerentia polluens. Quatenus est peccatum nos irae Dei addicens, ei respondet justificatio: quatenus vero est qualitas foeda nobis inhaerens, ei respondet sanctificatio. Tolli autem ista qualitas non potest, nisi prius tollatur ejus reatus. Itaque sanctificationem ordine naturae justificatio praecedit.
latin.127: Cum igitur corruptio duplicem illum respectum habeat, unum forensem, quo fit, ut, nisi condonetur, imputetur ad mortem; alterum moralem seu philosophicum, quo subjectum reddit habile ad peccandum, duplici nobis remedio opus fuit, imputatione justitiae Christi, quae mederetur reatui corruptionis, & vi Spiritus, qua e subjecto revelleretur. Nonne orthodoxa est haec doctrina, & ab omnibus purioribus Ecclesiis confessa? Miror igitur eam doctrinam a D. Garissolio hoc loco fuisse negatam. Quanquam id non est admodum mirandum. Vix enim fieri potest, quin in hunc scopulum incurrant ij, qui antecedentem imputationem probare student.
latin.128: Caeterum necessaria est imputatio justitiae non modo ut a reatu vitii inhaerentis, verum etiam ut ab omnibus aliis nostris peccatis justificemur. Id enim quod Deus gratificatur est ex multis lapsibus ad justificationem. Rom.5.16.
latin.129: Possem etiam hanc rationem in suum autorem retorquere. Nam si ubi nullum est malum, nullo opus est remedio, & nullum sit malum, si nullus sit in nobis propter Adae inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, & cur sit in nobis iste reatus vera & unica causa est Dei voluntas, non intelligo quae sit imputatae justitiae necessitas. Abstineat modo Deus ab imputatione primi Adae peccati quemadmodum sibi temperat ab aliorum peccatorum, vel ipsius Adami, vel nostrorum majorum, imputatione, nullum erit malum, nec opus erit remedio. Nulla enim est causa, si D. Garissolio fides habetur, cur Deus illud peccatum nobis potius quam alia peccata, vel Adami, vel aliorum parentum, imputet, praeter unam eius voluntatem. Cum ergo id pendeat ab eius voluntate ut imputet, vel non imputet, quid opus fuit, Christum tam dira pati, ut posset nobis illud peccatum non imputari?
latin.130: Possem etiam hoc loco contradictionem Domino Garissolio objicere. Ait enim, si nullus sit reatus prior corruptione, non esse opus imputata Christi justitia, & tamen alibi fatetur esse imputationem, & reatum corruptione posteriorem. Huic reatui qui corruptionem sequitur, quod justa proportione remedium respondet? sanctificatio? non opponitur proprie reatui. Justitia Christi imputata? Haec igitur, posita imputatione consequente seu mediata, nobis necessaria est. Itaque non labefactatur a Placeo doctrina de justitia Christi imputata: agnoscit enim imputationem & reatum consequentem; atque adeo peccatum originale, & satisfactionis Christi necessitatem, nihilque habet cum erroribus Socinianorum, Arminianorum &c, conjunctum.

pass_a.125: There remains his last reason, drawn from the imputation of Christ's justice. He frames it thus: Whatever overturns or weakens the doctrine of imputed Christ's justice is not to be admitted or tolerated, but wholly removed and rejected. But by the dogma of Non-imputation of Adam's sin, the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's justice is certainly weakened not a little, since from denial of the former the easiest slip is to denial of the latter. For since in Christ as a second Adam we have a most certain remedy against the evils and damages brought upon the human race from the first Adam; and a remedy ought to answer in just proportion to the diseases it is prepared to heal; whoever thinks we draw from Adam no damage besides native corruption, and will set over against that corruption the gift of sanctification, will easily come to this view: that there is in us no reatus prior to our original blot on account of Adam's disobedience, and that there is no need of any imputation of Christ's justice that would precede sanctification in the order of nature — because where there is no evil, there is also no need of a remedy.
pass_a.126: I deny that the dogma of Non-imputation of Adam's sin, antecedent or immediate, in any way weakens the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's justice; and it grieves me greatly to see a learned man, in order to prove that, desert the doctrine of the reatus of native corruption, declared and confirmed by the public confessions of faith of the Protestant churches. Native corruption can be viewed in two ways: one forensic, the other moral. In the former way it is considered as sin sufficient for damning us; in the latter as a quality polluting us by its inherence. Insofar as it is sin adjudging us to God's wrath, justification answers it; insofar as it is a foul quality inhering in us, sanctification answers it. But that quality cannot be taken away unless its reatus is first taken away. Therefore justification precedes sanctification in the order of nature.
pass_a.127: Since therefore corruption has that double respect — one forensic, whereby unless it is forgiven it is imputed unto death; the other moral or philosophical, whereby it makes the subject fit for sinning — we needed a double remedy: the imputation of Christ's justice to heal the reatus of corruption, and the power of the Spirit by which it would be torn out of the subject. Is this doctrine not orthodox, and confessed by all the purer churches? I marvel therefore that this doctrine was denied by D. Garissoles in this place. Though that is not greatly to be wondered at. For scarcely can it happen that those who labor to prove antecedent imputation do not run upon this rock.
pass_a.128: Besides, the imputation of justice is necessary not only that we may be justified from the reatus of inhering vice, but also from all our other sins. For that which God freely grants is justification from many falls. Romans 5:16.
pass_a.129: I could also turn this reason back upon its author. For if where there is no evil there is no need of a remedy, and there is no evil if there is in us no reatus prior to our original blot on account of Adam's disobedience, and the true and only cause why that reatus is in us is God's will — I do not understand what necessity there is of imputed justice. Let God only abstain from imputing the first Adam's sin, as He refrains from imputing other sins, whether Adam's own or our ancestors', and there will be no evil, nor need of a remedy. For there is no cause, if Garissoles is believed, why God should impute that sin to us rather than other sins, whether Adam's or other parents', except His will alone. Since therefore it hangs on His will whether to impute or not, what need was there that Christ suffer so dreadfully so that that sin might not be imputed to us?
pass_a.130: I could also in this place object a contradiction to Lord Garissoles. For he says that if there is no reatus prior to corruption, there is no need of imputed Christ's justice, and yet elsewhere he admits there is an imputation and a reatus posterior to corruption. To this reatus which follows corruption, what remedy answers in just proportion? Sanctification? It is not properly opposed to reatus. Imputed Christ's justice? This therefore, once consequent or mediate imputation is granted, is necessary for us. So the doctrine of imputed Christ's justice is not weakened by Placeus: for he acknowledges consequent imputation and reatus; and thus original sin and the necessity of Christ's satisfaction, and has nothing in common with the errors of Socinians, Arminians, and the like.

125: His last argument remains, drawn from the imputation of Christ’s justice. He puts it this way: anything that overturns or shakes the teaching of Christ’s imputed righteousness must not be allowed or endured, but must be rooted out and cast off entirely. Yet the dogma that Adam’s sin is not imputed, he says, certainly shakes that teaching more than a little — because denying the first makes denying the second an easy slide. Since in Christ, the second Adam, we have a sure remedy against the evils and losses the first Adam brought on the human race, and a remedy ought to match the diseases it is meant to heal, anyone who thinks we inherit from Adam nothing worse than native corruption — and who sets sanctification over against that corruption — will soon conclude that we have no guilt earlier than our original stain from Adam’s disobedience, and that we need no imputation of Christ’s justice ahead of sanctification in nature’s order: where there is no evil, no remedy is needed.
126: I deny that refusing antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam’s sin weakens, in any way, the doctrine of Christ’s imputed justice. It pains me to watch a learned man, for the sake of his proof, abandon the teaching that native corruption carries guilt — a teaching the Protestant churches have stated and sealed in their public confessions. Native corruption can be read two ways: forensically, or morally. Forensically it is sin enough to damn us; morally it is a quality that fouls us by clinging in us. As sin that binds us under God’s wrath, justification answers it; as a foul quality inhering in us, sanctification answers it. That quality cannot be removed until its guilt is removed first. So in nature’s order, justification comes before sanctification.
127: Corruption therefore wears a double face: forensic — so that unless it is forgiven it is charged to death — and moral or philosophical, making the subject ready to sin. We therefore needed a double cure: Christ’s justice imputed to heal corruption’s guilt, and the Spirit’s power to tear the blot out of the subject. Is this not orthodox teaching, confessed by all the purer churches? I am astonished that D. Garissoles denied it here — though the astonishment should not run deep. Those who press antecedent imputation almost cannot help striking this reef.
128: Moreover, the imputation of justice is needed not only to clear us of the guilt of the vice that inheres, but also to justify us from all our other sins. What God freely grants is justification from many falls (Rom. 5:16).
129: I can turn the argument on its maker. If no evil means no need of a remedy, and there is no evil unless we carry a guilt earlier than our original stain from Adam’s disobedience, and the sole true cause of that guilt in us is God’s will — then I cannot see why imputed justice is necessary at all. Let God simply withhold imputation of the first Adam’s sin, as He already withholds imputation of other sins — Adam’s own, or our forefathers’ — and there will be no evil and no need of a remedy. On Garissoles’s account there is no reason God should charge us with that sin rather than with Adam’s other sins or other parents’ sins, except His bare will. If imputing or not imputing hangs on that will alone, why did Christ have to suffer such horrors so that this sin might not be charged to us?
130: I can also charge Lord Garissoles with a contradiction here. He says that if no guilt precedes corruption, we do not need Christ’s imputed justice; yet elsewhere he admits an imputation and a guilt that follow corruption. What matching remedy answers that later guilt? Sanctification? It does not properly stand against guilt. Christ’s imputed justice? Once consequent or mediate imputation is granted, that justice is what we need. So Placeus does not shake the doctrine of Christ’s imputed righteousness: he owns consequent imputation and guilt, and with them original sin and the need for Christ’s satisfaction — and he shares nothing with Socinian, Arminian, and kindred errors.
